content: The chloride ion is created when a chlorine atom gains one electron, resulting in the formation of a negatively charged ion, denoted as Cl−. Salts derived from hydrochloric acid (HCl) contain chloride ions and are commonly referred to as chlorides. A well-known example is table salt, chemically known as sodium chloride (NaCl). When dissolved in water, sodium chloride dissociates into sodium ions (Na+) and chloride ions (Cl−). The term chloride can also describe chemical compounds in which one or more chlorine atoms are covalently bonded within the molecule. These compounds can be either inorganic or organic in nature. The simplest example of an inorganic covalently bonded chloride is hydrogen chloride (HCl). An example of an organic covalently bonded chloride, also known as an organochloride, is chloromethane (CH3Cl), commonly referred to as methyl chloride. Other examples of inorganic covalently bonded chlorides include phosphorus trichloride (PCl3), phosphorus pentachloride (PCl5), and thionyl chloride (SOCl2). These compounds are reactive chlorinating agents frequently used in laboratory settings. Additionally, disulfur dichloride (S2Cl2) is another inorganic chloride, utilized in the vulcanization process of rubber. Human Health Chloride ions play critical roles in human physiology. In the central nervous system, the inhibitory effects of glycine and certain actions of gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA) depend on the influx of chloride ions (Cl−) into specific neurons. Furthermore, the chloride-bicarbonate exchanger, a biological transport protein, relies on chloride ions to enhance the blood's capacity to carry carbon dioxide in the form of bicarbonate ions. The North American Dietary Reference Intake recommends a daily chloride intake of 2300 to 3600 mg for 25-year-old males. Other Applications Chloride serves as a reliable chemical indicator for detecting fecal contamination in river and groundwater systems. This is because chloride is a non-reactive solute and is commonly found in sewage, making it a ubiquitous marker for such contamination.
